newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly vows to okay its own FY 1998 budget.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly vows to okay its own FY 1998 budget.

text.p: The New York State Assembly, which is led by Democrats, vowed to be the first house to approve a new budget, but talks to iron out differences with the Senate and Gov George Pataki seemed suspended Wednesday.

Asked if the Assembly and the governor, a Republican, were negotiating a huge difference over how much extra revenues they expect New York State to get, a spokeswoman for Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, said: "He (Pataki) really hasn't engaged yet."

The consensus estimate of revenues was due on March 10, and the failure of the governor and the two branches of the legislature to agree on one was a sign their efforts to reacht a budget by the April 1 due date were in jeopardy.
The state last year set a national record for late budgets. Both houses were expected to soon approve a $9.9 billion contingency budget to keep the state government running through May 9.

The governor took on both the Assembly Speaker and a potential Democrat challenger for governor, State Comptroller, H. Carl McCall, who late last week said that the fight over how much of a windfall the state would collect in fiscal 1997 and 1998 had narrowed to $1.3 billion--an estimate that could be met though relying on it added to the budget's risk. Wall Street banks and brokers are expected to produce handsome profits for themselves and big tax revenues for the state.

Pataki, saying he was "astounded" by what he called McCall's statement that various revenue estimates were reasonable, told reporters in Albany that: "I am also waiting for Comptroller McCall to take a look at the $4.97 billion structural imbalance in the 1998-1999 fiscal year that we believe exists, and to hear his comments on that."
A spokesman for McCall had no immediate response.
The governor, who predicted the state would only get about $650 million more than it had anticipated by the end of the 1998 fiscal year, was referring to the Assembly's budget.

The Assembly Speaker's spokeswoman, Patricia Lynch, disputed Pataki's latest criticisms, saying Silver was "very comfortable" with the Assembly's estimates and that the Assembly's budget was balanced.

"This house will have passed a timely and balanced budget," she said, predicting the Assembly's own pact would be approved by the April 1 deadline. Adding it was up to the Senate to approve its own version, she said: "Maybe we need to do a conference."
Little progress was made on hotly contested rent control rules, whose expiry on June 15 is expected to be used as a weapon against the Speaker as the rules mainly affect New York City residents.

While the Republican Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, has proposed returning to a market-based system with some protections for senior citizens, for example, the Speaker wants the regulations extended. And Pataki said he had yet to decide whether to offer his own plan or try to help the Senate and Assembly resolve their fight.

Asked if he would favor phasing out rent contral provided needy residents were protected, Pataki replied: "I didn't say that. I will be glad to outline it (a plan) in detail if ultimately that is in the interest of advancing the resolution of this problem."

The governor in prepared remarks harshly criticized the Assembly's $5.5 billion, five-year education plan for failing to reduce high property taxes, which many districts outside New York City to fund schools.
Pataki said: "The Assembly just doesn't get it--New York's property taxes are too high."

Finally, the governor blasted the Assembly plan to reduce clothing sales taxes because its budget did not include a one-week moratorium that proved widely popular in January, and postponned reductions until the 1998 fiscal year.

"So I think we should look, as the Senate has proposed, to provide some real school tax relief, and not just school tax relief but sales tax relief this year, and work to get rid of the sales tax on clothing," Pataki said.
Pataki added: "But I would like to see us this year be in a position over a period of time, in a fiscally responsible way, to get rid of it (clothing sales taxes)."
